```
def q(x,Lb,l,k=12):
    t=cKDTree(x%Lb,boxsize=Lb); d,j=t.query(x%Lb,k=k+1); v=x[j[:,1:]]-x[:,None,:]; v-=Lb*np.round(v/Lb)
    r=np.linalg.norm(v,axis=2); th=np.arccos(v[...,2]/r); ph=np.arctan2(v[...,1],v[...,0])
    Y=np.array([sph_harm(m,l,ph,th).mean(1) for m in range(-l,l+1)])
```

```
def q(x,Lb,l,k=12):
    t=cKDTree(x%Lb,boxsize=Lb); d,j=t.query(x%Lb,k=k+1); v=x[j[:,1:]]-x[:,None,:]; v-=Lb*np.round(v/Lb)
    r=np.linalg.norm(v,axis=2); th=np.arccos(v[...,2]/r); ph=np.arctan2(v[...,1],v[...,0])
    Y=np.array([sph_harm_y(l,m,th,ph).mean(1) for m in range(-l,l+1)])
    return np.sqrt(4*np.pi/(2*l+1)*(abs(Y)**2).sum(0))
```

```
/* ----------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

#ifdef PAIR_CLASS
// clang-format off
PairStyle(vasp,PairVASP);
// clang-format on
#else

#ifndef LMP_PAIR_VASP_H
#define LMP_PAIR_VASP_H

#include "pair.h"

namespace vaspml {
  class InterfaceLAMMPS;
}

namespace LAMMPS_NS {

class PairVASP : public Pair {

 public:
  PairVASP(class LAMMPS *);
  ~PairVASP() override;
  void compute(int, int) override;
  void settings(int, char **) override;
  void coeff(int, char **) override;
  void init_style() override;
  double init_one(int, int) override;

 protected:
  virtual void allocate();

  double cutoff;
  vaspml::InterfaceLAMMPS *vasp;

};

} // namespace LAMMPS_NS

#endif
#endif
PairVASP::PairVASP(LAMMPS *lmp) : Pair(lmp)
{
  if (lmp->citeme) lmp->citeme->add(cite_user_vaspml_package);

  single_enable = 0;
  restartinfo = 0;
  one_coeff = 1;
  manybody_flag = 1;
  //unit_convert_flag = utils::get_supported_conversions(utils::ENERGY);

  vasp = new vaspml::InterfaceLAMMPS();
}

/* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   check if allocated, since class can be destructed when incomplete
------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

PairVASP::~PairVASP()
{
  delete vasp;
  memory->destroy(setflag);
  memory->destroy(cutsq);
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------- */

void PairVASP::allocate()
{
  allocated = 1;
  int n = atom->ntypes;

  memory->create(setflag,n+1,n+1,"pair:setflag");
  memory->create(cutsq,n+1,n+1,"pair:cutsq");
  map = new int[n+1];
}

/* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
   global settings
------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

void PairVASP::settings(int narg, char **arg)
```

```
// Shim compiled with the VASPml compiler/flags (2026-11-17, Anelasticity hcp-Fe set-up).
// InterfaceLAMMPS (VASPml 6.6.0) never calls global::parallel.init(), so in LAMMPS the library always runs the
// "classic" CPU path (palgo = off), even when it is compiled with nvc++ -stdpar=gpu. This exposes init() through a
// plain C symbol so the LAMMPS plugin (compiled with g++) can select the parallel algorithm (off|serial|threads|gpu).
#include "ParallelEnvironment.hpp"
#include <cstdio>
#include <stdexcept>

extern "C" int vaspml_set_palgo(const char* palgo)
{
    try
    {
        vaspml::global::parallel.init(palgo);
    }
    catch (const std::exception& e)
    {
        std::fprintf(stderr, "vaspml_set_palgo(%s) failed: %s\n", palgo, e.what());
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

extern "C" const char* vaspml_supported_palgos()
{
    static std::string s;
    s = vaspml::global::parallel.supported();
    return s.c_str();
}
EOF
```

### Claude (11-17 10:03)

Both builds are submitted (VASP 6.6.0). Nothing has been checked yet: neither build has finished, so there are no results.

**Can VASP force fields run on GPUs in LAMMPS?** Probably, but not out of the box.
- VASP's 6.6.0 ML library contains GPU code that the documentation doesn't mention. It turns on when the library is compiled with the NVIDIA compiler.
- However, the LAMMPS interface never switches it on. Even a GPU-compiled library would run on the CPU inside LAMMPS.
- I work around this with a small wrapper that selects the GPU mode when LAMMPS starts. It is controlled by an environment variable, `VASPML_PALGO=gpu`. No VASP source is changed.

**The GPU code goes into the LAMMPS you already use (job 7056604, running).**
- I'm building `pair_style vasp` as a plugin for the production LAMMPS in deepmd_py311, which already has DeePMD and PLUMED. You load it in an input with `plugin load /groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS_VASP/plugin/vaspplugin.so`.
- The ML library is compiled with NVHPC 23.9 for the P100 and newer cards. The `pair_vasp` source is VASP's own file, unchanged, compiled against your LAMMPS headers.
- The same plugin runs on CPU if the variable is left unset.
- I keep it out of the folder LAMMPS loads plugins from automatically, so your DeePMD runs are unaffected.

**The CPU build (job 7056606, pending in the queue)** is the documented VASP route: Intel compilers and MKL, with a few extra standard LAMMPS packages. It will also be linked as `~/bin/lmp_mpi_vasp`. Because the VASP ML library was compiled for Ice Lake, it runs on Ice Lake or newer nodes only.

**Next:** when the builds finish I'll run the checks set up in `LAMMPS/VASP/Fe/plugin_test`:
- Recompute the first step of your 8192-atom sample with both builds. Your 2025 log has P = 2945557.3 bar and enthalpy = 54113.194 eV.
- Compare the forces from the CPU and GPU versions.
- Time both against the sample's 6.5 steps/s.

**Your sample run isn't hcp.** Its starting cell (`end.pos.start`) is a crystallized quench: mixed close-packed with defects, not a single hcp crystal. So the 0.15 % volume drop near 5300–5600 K is more likely annealing or grain growth than a phase change. For the inner-core runs we should build a perfect hcp cell.

**Also:**
- There is already an older CPU LAMMPS with `pair_style vasp` from 2026‑03‑31 at `LAMMPS_VASP/lammps/build/lmp`. I've left it untouched.
- I still need to know where the training data (`ML_AB`) for this `ML_FF` is. I want to confirm it covers 300–350 GPa and 5000–7000 K.

The build scripts and a README are in `~/Claude/tools/vasp_lammps/`, and INPROGRESS §1 and §3 are updated.

### Claude (11-17 10:07)

The first GPU build compiled the ML library but failed when linking the plugin, and I've resubmitted it with a fix (job 7056862). The CPU build (job 7056606) is still waiting for an Ice Lake node. Nothing has been tested yet.

**Why the GPU link failed.** VASP's GPU code checks for a compiler macro name used by newer NVIDIA compilers. NVHPC 23.9, the version on the cluster, defines the same thing under an older name.
- As a result, VASP's small helper functions were never compiled for the GPU. The link then stopped at undefined GPU references.
- VASP's own build files don't cover GPU builds of the ML library, so this route is unsupported territory.

**The fix.** I define the newer macro name by hand in the GPU build settings (`-D__NVCOMPILER_STDPAR_GPU=1`) and rebuild the library from clean.
- I compiled two of the GPU source files with this flag as a test. The GPU versions of the functions are now produced, where before there were none.
- If 23.9 causes further trouble, the fallback is to install a newer NVHPC in your space. It is a large download, so I'd ask you first.

**Next.** Once both builds finish I'll run the checks in `LAMMPS/VASP/Fe/plugin_test`:
- Recompute the first step of your 8192-atom sample run with each build. Your 2025 log has P = 2945557.3 bar and enthalpy = 54113.194 eV.
- Compare the forces from the CPU and GPU builds.
- Time both against the sample's 6.5 steps/s.

The fix is noted in `~/Claude/tools/vasp_lammps/makefile.include.gpu`.

**Tool `Bash`** — Append hcp Fe section to the 11-17 restart

```
cat >> /resnick/home/recohen/Claude/Anelasticity/ANELASTICITY_RESTART_2026-11-17.md <<'EOF'

## 7. hcp Fe with the VASP MLFF (added 11-17 ≈ 10:30; RC: "Go ahead and build both with 6.6.0 now", then VASP 6.6.1 arrived)
Tools, scripts and README: `/resnick/home/recohen/Claude/tools/vasp_lammps/`; read the README first.
- **GPU in LAMMPS.** VASPml has an NVIDIA stdpar/OpenACC/cuBLAS prediction path, but `InterfaceLAMMPS` never calls `global::parallel.init()`, so LAMMPS always runs the CPU path.
```

### Claude (11-17 10:16)

You don't need to end this session or start a new one for the builds. Everything is running as batch jobs from here, and I've updated the restart notes (§7 of `ANELASTICITY_RESTART_2026-11-17.md`) and INPROGRESS in case the session ends. An interactive GPU session would only help if the GPU test keeps failing. If you start one, give me its job ID and I can run tests inside it directly.

**Your training set doesn't contain hcp.** The refit `ML_FF` in `VASP/Fe/bcc/ML/Orthogonal/P300GPa` is identical to the one your sample run used.
- It has 913 configurations, all 128-atom cells started from bcc, so hcp was never deliberately sampled.
- The low-force configurations are bcc; the hotter ones are hot bcc and liquid.
- Volumes are 6.6–7.5 Å³/atom and DFT pressures 250–320 GPa, about 265–335 GPa once the thermal part at ~6000 K is added. So 350 GPa is at or past the edge of what the force field has seen.

Running hcp Fe at 300–350 GPa with this force field would be extrapolating. I recommend extending the training with on-the-fly hcp runs in 6.6.1 first: 300–350 GPa, 5000–7000 K, and some liquid. I'll put a proposal with costs in INPROGRESS for you to approve.

**VASP 6.6.1** is unpacked in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/VASP/VASP/vasp.6.6.1`, using your 6.6.0 Intel settings (`makefile.include` copied over).
- The first build (std, gam, ncl) failed because building all three at once tripped over a shared module file. It is now rebuilding one version at a time (job 7057228).
- The CPU LAMMPS build with `pair_style vasp` is queued to start when that finishes (job 7057229).
- The 6.6.1 ML library differs from 6.6.0 only in files we don't use. VASP's LAMMPS branch is still the 6.6.0 one.

**GPU plugin for your existing LAMMPS** (the one with DeePMD and PLUMED): it builds and loads, but hasn't run a step yet.
- It needed three fixes for the cluster's NVIDIA compiler (23.9): two compiler settings, plus linking the compiler's Fortran runtime, which its LAPACK needs.
- Two earlier test jobs also failed on bugs in my test input, now fixed.
- The check on the 8192-atom sample is queued (job 7057289). It compares the step-0 pressure, enthalpy and forces against your 2025 log and against the CPU path, then times it.
- Once that passes, I'll rebuild the plugin from the 6.6.1 source.

### Claude (11-17 10:17)

I've hit a new problem with the GPU plugin and am testing a fix (job 7057457, queued). The VASP 6.6.1 rebuild (job 7057228) is running, and the CPU LAMMPS build (job 7057229) will start when it finishes.

**What failed.** The plugin now loads into your production LAMMPS, but the test crashed with `free(): invalid pointer` before reading the structure. It crashed both in GPU mode and when forced onto the CPU path.

**Likely cause.** On the P100, the GPU code puts its memory in GPU-shared ("managed") memory. The NVIDIA runtime library that knows how to free that memory loads only with the plugin, after LAMMPS has started. So the system's standard memory routines handle some of those frees and reject the pointers.

**Fix being tested.** The test now preloads that NVIDIA library (`libnvhpcmanaux.so`, set with `LD_PRELOAD`) so it handles every free from the start. If that doesn't work, the fallback is to compile `pair_vasp` and the plugin wrapper with the NVIDIA compiler as well.

Once a test gets past step 0, I'll compare its pressure, enthalpy and forces with your 2025 log and with the CPU path, and time it against the sample's 6.5 steps/s.

### Claude (11-17 10:18)

The GPU plugin hasn't produced a result yet. My first fix crashed at startup, and a second attempt (job 7057545) is queued.

**What failed:**
- **First run.** The plugin loaded into your LAMMPS, but the run crashed with `free(): invalid pointer` before reading the structure. It crashed both in GPU mode and when forced onto the CPU path. This fits the memory mismatch I described last time.
- **Preloading NVIDIA's memory library.** Both runs stopped at startup with `undefined symbol: __pgi_uacc_cuda_initdinfoflags`. That library needs other NVIDIA runtime libraries that weren't loaded with it.

**Now testing:** `LD_PRELOAD=vaspplugin.so` for the LAMMPS process only. That puts the plugin's whole chain of NVIDIA libraries ahead of the system ones, so a single memory handler serves the whole run.

**If that fails too,** I'll compile `pair_vasp` and the plugin wrapper with the NVIDIA compiler as well, so all the memory handling comes from one compiler.

The VASP 6.6.1 build (job 7057228) is running, and the CPU LAMMPS build (job 7057229) starts when it finishes.

### Claude (11-17 10:20)

The GPU plugin still crashes with `free(): invalid pointer`, and loading it before LAMMPS starts didn't help. With that change it now dies before LAMMPS even prints its banner. So the bad free happens while the plugin's own code is being set up, before any LAMMPS work.

That points to a mismatch in how memory is handled between NVIDIA-compiled and GNU-compiled code. Rather than keep guessing, I've submitted a short debugger job on a P100 (job 7057633). It records where the crash happens in two cases: loading the plugin from the LAMMPS input, and loading it before LAMMPS starts. The backtrace will show which code does the bad free, and I'll fix the build from that.

The VASP 6.6.1 build (job 7057228) is still running. The CPU LAMMPS build (job 7057229) starts when it finishes, and the CPU path doesn't involve the NVIDIA compiler.

### Claude (11-17 10:23)

The GPU plugin still hasn't run a step. A debugger run found the crash, and a fixed test is queued (job 7057847). Separately, VASP 6.6.1 `vasp_std` is built, and `gam` and `ncl` are being retried after a build race.

**GPU plugin crash: cause found**
- The debugger shows the abort happens while the plugin is being loaded. It comes from VASP's own LAMMPS interface code (`InterfaceLAMMPS.cpp`).
- Code built by the NVIDIA compiler takes memory from NVIDIA's managed pool, but the standard system `free()` releases it. Hence `free(): invalid pointer`.
- NVIDIA ships its own `free()` (in `libnvhpcmanaux.so`) that handles that memory, but it only works if it is found before the system one.
- My earlier attempts loaded it too late, or without the libraries it depends on. The new test loads `libnvhpcmanaux.so` and the plugin together before LAMMPS starts.
- If this works, every GPU run will need that `LD_PRELOAD` line, and I'll write it into the run scripts. The check then compares step-0 pressure, enthalpy and forces with your 2025 log and the CPU path, and times it.

**VASP 6.6.1**
- `vasp_std` is built in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/VASP/VASP/vasp.6.6.1/bin`.
- `gam` failed with the same race in the library's Fortran modules as before, even with one version built at a time. It is a timing race, and `std` got through, so `gam` and `ncl` are being rebuilt with up to three tries each (job 7057874).

**CPU LAMMPS with `pair_style vasp`**
- Building now against 6.6.1's ML library, taken from the finished `std` build (job 7057900). The library is identical in all three VASP versions.

The GPU plugin now runs, and its first step matches your 2025 sample run. I don't have a speed yet: the 100-step timing run is still going (job 7057847).

**Step-0 check** on the 8192-atom sample, one P100, `VASPML_PALGO=gpu`:

| | 2025 log | GPU plugin | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pressure (bar) | 2945557.3 | 2945569.0 | +11.7 (4 parts per million) |
| Enthalpy (eV) | 54113.194 | 54113.684 | +0.49 (0.06 meV/atom) |

- Both differences are tiny. The old binary was built from an older VASP, so I don't treat them as an error yet.
- The atom-by-atom force comparison waits for the CPU build (job 7057900).

**What made it work.** The crash was a memory mismatch between NVIDIA-compiled and standard code. Every GPU run therefore has to start LAMMPS with two libraries preloaded, `libnvhpcmanaux.so` and the plugin:

```
env LD_PRELOAD=/central/software9/external/nvhpc/23.9/Linux_x86_64/23.9/compilers/lib/libnvhpcmanaux.so:/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS_VASP/plugin/vaspplugin.so lmp -in ...
```

The input then needs `plugin load /groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS_VASP/plugin/vaspplugin.so` before `pair_style vasp`. The working script is `LAMMPS/VASP/Fe/plugin_test/gpu_check.sh`.

**Possible speed problem.** After about 2 minutes the GPU run hadn't printed step 10. If that holds, it is slower than your 32-core CPU run (6.5 steps/s).

- The rest of `gpu_check.sh`: the plugin with the GPU off on 8 cores, for a CPU-path comparison.
- The CPU LAMMPS build (job 7057900).

### Claude (11-17 10:30)

The GPU plugin now runs correctly in your production LAMMPS, but on a P100 it is slow: 0.31 steps/s for the 8192-atom sample, about 20× slower than one CPU node.

**Accuracy.** Step 0 matches your 2025 log closely:

| | 2025 log | plugin |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure (bar) | 2945557.3 | 2945569.0 |
| Enthalpy (eV) | 54113.194 | 54113.684 |

That is 4 parts per million in pressure and 0.06 meV/atom in enthalpy. The 2025 run used an older VASP ML library, so a difference this size is not a concern.

The plugin's GPU and CPU paths give the same energy to 2 μeV, and forces differ by at most 1×10⁻⁷ eV/Å. Total energy is conserved to 1.5 meV over 100 constant-energy steps.

**Speed:**

| run | steps/s |
|---|---|
| GPU path, 1 P100 | **0.31** |
| CPU path of the same plugin, 8 Broadwell cores | 0.98 |
| your 2025 run, Intel CPU build, 32 ranks × 2 threads | 6.47 |

As it stands, the GPU route is not useful on P100s. I'm profiling it with NVIDIA's profiler (job 7058218) to see whether the GPU is actually busy or the time goes to moving data between CPU and GPU memory every step. That decides whether it can be fixed, or whether the CPU build is the production route for Fe. Newer GPUs could also change the picture, but on P100s the CPU nodes win.

**One requirement for any plugin run.** LAMMPS has to be started as `env LD_PRELOAD=.../compilers/lib/libnvhpcmanaux.so:/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS_VASP/plugin/vaspplugin.so lmp ...`. NVIDIA's own memory-freeing routine must load before the system one, or the run aborts while loading the plugin. The working script is `LAMMPS/VASP/Fe/plugin_test/gpu_check.sh`, and the details are in `~/Claude/tools/vasp_lammps/README.md`.

**Still building:**
- The CPU LAMMPS with `pair_style vasp`, against the VASP 6.6.1 ML library (job 7057900).
- VASP 6.6.1 `gam` and `ncl` (job 7057874); `vasp_std` is already built.

### Claude (11-17 10:37)

Yes, it really runs on the GPU, but it uses it badly. I sampled `nvidia-smi dmon` every 2 s during a 20-step run, which shows the same information as `nvidia-smi -l 60` at a finer interval, and also ran NVIDIA's profiler (`nsys`).

**GPU usage (`nvidia-smi dmon`):**
- Compute utilization averaged 20 %, jumping between 0 and 100 %.
- GPU memory grew from 0.3 GB to 15.5 GB of the P100's 16 GB.
- Both drop back to zero when the run ends.

**Where the time goes**, per force call (about 3 s each, 0.35 steps/s):
- About 1 s is VASP's own GPU kernels, many of them taking 0.1–0.4 s each.
- About 5 GB of data moves back and forth between CPU and GPU memory in roughly 100,000 small transfers. That costs at least 0.5 s, plus page-fault overhead. The CPU-side code touches the shared arrays between kernels, so the data keeps migrating. Pascal cards like the P100 handle this especially slowly.
- There are about 24,600 tiny GPU math calls (cuBLAS `axpy`) and about 1,400 memory allocations and frees.

So VASP's GPU path works and gives the right answers (identical to the CPU path to 1×10⁻⁷ eV/Å), but on a P100 it is about 20× slower than one CPU node. For the Fe runs I recommend the CPU build. Newer GPUs (H100/H200) might do much better, but that's untested; a 10-minute H200 test would settle it if you want it.

**VASP 6.6.1:** `vasp_std`, `vasp_gam` and `vasp_ncl` are built in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/VASP/VASP/vasp.6.6.1/bin`.

**CPU LAMMPS:** my first build had actually run before I cancelled it, so it was linked against the 6.6.0 ML library. I deleted it and am rebuilding cleanly against the 6.6.1 library (job 7058476). The CPU check follows automatically (job 7058477) and will give step-0 pressure and forces compared with the GPU numbers, plus steps/s on 32 × 2 Ice Lake cores.

After that I'll propose the hcp training runs with VASP 6.6.1, with costs, since the current force field has no hcp in it.

The profile files (`dmon.txt`, `nsys_stats.txt`, `prof_gpu.nsys-rep`) are in `/groups/carnegie_poc/rcohen/LAMMPS/VASP/Fe/plugin_test/`, and the full log is in `~/Claude/tools/vasp_lammps/README.md`.
